These figures are approximate, from a manual review of the rows. Denials are a small minority in every group. Rough denial rates: Hispanic or Latino about 10-11%, White about 7-8%, Asian about 7%, Black or African American about 8% (small sample). The clearest driver of denial is debt-to-income ratio. Hispanic applicants appear more often in those high-DTI bands among the denials, which accounts for much of their higher raw denial rate. Other denials match identifiable risk factors such as LTV of 100% or more (e.g., 300 or 102), zero or very low reported income, or very small loans. Similar high-risk applicants are denied across White, Asian, Hispanic and Black groups, and some high-DTI applicants of different races, including minority applicants, were approved. Sex shows no consistent pattern: Male, Female and Joint applicants are all denied at broadly similar rates. A modest raw disparity exists for Hispanic applicants, but it largely tracks financial risk variables. This summary data cannot separate discrimination from risk factors such as credit score, which is not included, so the evidence is not conclusive either way.

Denial rates are low for every racial group, roughly 6-10% based on a manual review, and denials occur among White, Asian, Hispanic and Black applicants alike. Small gaps exist (Black and Hispanic applicants appear slightly more often among denials than White or Asian applicants), but most minority denials coincide with clear risk factors: debt-to-income ratios of 50%-60% or above 60%, loan-to-value ratios near or above 95-100%, or very low or zero income. High-DTI applicants are treated similarly across races. White applicants with DTI of 50% or more were frequently denied (about 16 denials), and Hispanic applicants in those bands were also mixed (several approved at 50%-60%; most denied above 60%). Comparable profiles, such as high LTV with DTI of 45-49, are approved across all races. The data shows no consistent disparity unexplained by credit factors. However, this is observational data without credit scores or formal statistical controls, so discrimination cannot be ruled out with certainty.

Based on approximate tallies of this sample (not an exact statistical test), raw denial rates are modestly higher for Black (roughly 11 denials out of about 75 applicants, ~14%) and Hispanic (~11-12%) applicants than for White and Asian applicants (~7-8%). However, the Black subgroup is small, so its rate is statistically unstable. Most denials across all races cluster in high-risk profiles: debt-to-income of 50%-60% or >60%, loan-to-value at or above ~95-100%, or very low or zero income. Several Black and Hispanic denials fall into these categories, such as DTI 50%-60% or >60%, LTV 100-131%, or income of $40-60k on $485k-$605k loans. Applicants of all races with similar credit risk factors, including White and Asian applicants with DTI >60%, were also denied at high rates. The data shows raw outcome disparities but does not demonstrate differential treatment after accounting for DTI, LTV and income. Key underwriting variables such as credit score are also missing, so discrimination can neither be confirmed nor ruled out from this data alone. A conclusive answer would require a controlled analysis, such as logistic regression on denial with race plus risk factors.

Counts below are approximate, from a manual review of roughly 1,500 records. The overall denial rate is about 7-8%, and every racial group (White, Asian, Hispanic or Latino, Black or African American, Other) and every sex category (Male, Female, Joint) has both approvals and denials. Denials cluster around financial risk factors. A large share have DTI above 50% (the '50%-60%' and '>60%' bands), and those high-DTI bands are denied at much higher rates than '<20%' to '36%' applicants of any race. Other denials have LTV of 95-100% or more, very low income relative to the loan, or anomalous values (e.g., LTV 454, loan amount above property value). Hispanic and Black applicants show somewhat higher raw denial rates than White and Asian applicants, but they also more often have higher DTI, higher LTV and lower income. White applicants with similar profiles (e.g., DTI 50-60%) are also denied. Many minority applicants with DTI of 45-49% and LTV of 95%+ were approved. The data has no credit score, credit history, denial reasons or lender identifiers, and the small Black and Other groups make their rates unstable. Some raw gaps exist, but they are not shown to persist after accounting for financial factors, so the data does not establish discrimination.

The data shows a disparity but does not establish discrimination. Counts below are approximate, from a manual tally. Black or African American applicants (about 60 records) were denied about 10 times (roughly 17%), versus an estimated overall denial rate of roughly 8-9%. That gap is notable, but the Black sample is small, so it is only marginally significant. Several of those denials also have identifiable risk factors: DTI of 50%-60%, very small loans ($75K-$95K), low income ($42K), or LTV near 95-97%. Across all groups, denials concentrate in high-DTI applications (>60% and 50%-60% bands are denied at very high rates), which suggests DTI is the main observable driver. Denials also occur among White and Asian applicants with strong profiles, such as a White joint applicant with $1.35M income and DTI below 20%. Some Black denials look well-qualified on the available fields (for example, DTI 30%-36%, LTV 80, income $386K), which warrants review. However, the dataset lacks credit score, credit history, employment, and denial reasons, so the disparity cannot be attributed to race rather than unobserved factors. Conclusion: there is a statistical disparity for Black applicants that merits a controlled analysis (such as a regression on DTI, LTV, and income), but there is insufficient evidence to conclude discrimination.

The data shows a racial disparity in denials, but not proof of intentional discrimination. Counts are approximate, from a manual tally. Black or African American applicants: about 13 of roughly 60 were denied (about 20%). Only about 4 of the Black denials have high debt-to-income ratios (50%+ or >60%). The rest have DTIs of 30-49% and mostly high loan-to-value ratios (90-100%). Many applicants of other races with similar DTI and LTV profiles were approved, for example numerous White and Hispanic applicants with DTI 44-49 and LTV 95-97. With an expected denial rate near 7%, about 4 Black denials would be expected rather than 13, so the gap is unlikely to be chance. Limitations: the Black sample is small, and key underwriting variables such as credit score, employment and reserves are missing. Most denials in every group cluster at DTI above 50% or at unusual income values (0, negative, very low), which shows legitimate risk factors drive many decisions. The data supports a disparity in outcomes worth investigating but cannot confirm discrimination.

However, about half of the Black denials (6 of 11) involve clear underwriting risk factors: debt-to-income above 60%, debt-to-income of 50-60%, or a reported income of 0. Applicants with high debt-to-income are frequently denied regardless of race or sex, though not always; several White, Asian and Hispanic applicants in the 50-60% band were approved. The remaining Black denials (about 5) have moderate debt-to-income (37-47%). Similar unexplained denials also appear among White, Asian and Hispanic applicants with comparable profiles. Approval rates by sex (Male, Female, Joint) look broadly similar. The data also lacks key underwriting variables such as credit score, credit history, employment and assets. Because of that, and because the Black and Other groups are small, the observed gap cannot be attributed to race rather than legitimate risk factors. A regression or matched comparison controlling for debt-to-income, loan-to-value, income and loan amount would be needed to test for discrimination.

By approximate count, denials are spread across all racial and sex groups (White, Hispanic or Latino, Asian, Black, Other; Male, Female, Joint), and no group appears to be denied at a markedly higher rate than its share of applications. Denials cluster around financial risk factors rather than demographics. Applicants with debt-to-income ratios above 60% are denied in nearly every case, whatever their race (about 2 of roughly 30 such applications were originated). The 50%-60% DTI band also shows elevated denials. Several other denials involve negative or zero income, or loan-to-value ratios above 100%. Comparable applicants with lower DTI and normal income are approved at high rates in every group. However, this is observational data with no credit scores, credit history, or denial reasons, and some groups (Black, Other) have small samples. The data therefore cannot rule out subtle disparities. It also cannot establish that discrimination is absent, only that no clear pattern of it appears here.

Denials cluster around weak financial indicators: debt-to-income ratios of 50%-60% or above 60%, loan-to-value ratios near or above 95-100%, or very low or zero reported income. Applicants in all groups with similar weak profiles were also denied, and applicants in all groups with typical DTI (36-49%) and LTV (≤95%) were overwhelmingly approved. Black applicants show a somewhat higher raw denial rate, roughly 7 of about 60. That sample is small, and several of those denials involve DTI above 50%, LTV of 97-100% or more, or zero income. The data show no consistent disparity by race or sex that persists after accounting for DTI and LTV. However, it cannot rule out discrimination, because key factors such as credit score are missing and no formal statistical test was performed.
